topics.name: Vectors: Representation, Addition, Subtraction, and Resolution into Components
topics.summary: Vectors are quantities with both magnitude and direction, such as displacement, velocity, and force, represented as arrows or in component form using unit vectors \( \hat i \) and \( \hat j \) along the x- and y-axes. Any vector \( \vec A \) at angle \( \theta \) to the x-axis has components \( A_x=A\cos\theta \) and \( A_y=A\sin\theta \), and its magnitude is recovered via \( A=\sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2} \). Two vectors combine by the triangle or parallelogram law: the magnitude of their resultant is \( R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta} \), where \( \theta \) is the angle between them — this collapses to simple addition or subtraction of magnitudes only when the vectors are exactly parallel or antiparallel. Vector subtraction follows the same law with a minus sign instead, \( |\vec A-\vec B|=\sqrt{A^2+B^2-2AB\cos\theta} \). The direction of the resultant relative to \( \vec A \) is given by \( \tan\beta=\dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta} \). These resolution and combination skills underlie every other topic in this chapter, since almost every two-dimensional quantity is first broken into components before anything else can be done with it.
topics.worked_example: Two forces of magnitude \( 5 \) N and \( 3 \) N act at a point with an angle of \( 60^\circ \) between them. The resultant magnitude is \( R=\sqrt{5^2+3^2+2\times5\times3\times\cos60^\circ}=\sqrt{25+9+15}=\sqrt{49}=7 \) N.
common_mistakes: Adding or subtracting vector magnitudes directly without accounting for the angle between them — this is only valid when the vectors are exactly parallel or antiparallel.
Swapping \( \sin\theta \) and \( \cos\theta \) between the magnitude formula and the direction formula.
Forgetting to square the components before combining them into a magnitude, or forgetting the square root at the end.

topics.name: Motion in a Plane with Constant Velocity and Constant Acceleration
topics.summary: This topic extends one-dimensional kinematics into two dimensions by treating the x- and y-motions as completely independent. For constant velocity, displacement follows \( \vec s=\vec v\,t \); for constant acceleration, velocity and displacement follow \( \vec v=\vec u+\vec a\,t \) and \( \vec s=\vec u\,t+\dfrac12\vec a\,t^2 \), applied separately to each component. Average velocity over an interval is \( \vec v_{avg}=\Delta\vec r/\Delta t \), using the actual elapsed time, not just the later time reading. A key skill is recognizing that a single vector equation is really two independent scalar equations in disguise — finding when a specific component vanishes, or finding the direction of a resultant velocity or displacement, both require resolving into x- and y-parts first, and the direction of displacement is not generally the same as the direction of velocity. This framework is the foundation for projectile motion (where \( a_x=0 \) and \( a_y=-g \)) and for any multi-stage planar motion problem where the acceleration itself changes partway through.
topics.worked_example: A particle starts with velocity \( \vec u=1\,\hat i+1\,\hat j \) m/s and constant acceleration \( \vec a=4\,\hat i+6\,\hat j \) m/s\( ^2 \). After \( 1 \) s: \( s_x=1\times1+\dfrac12\times4\times1^2=3 \) m, \( s_y=1\times1+\dfrac12\times6\times1^2=4 \) m, so \( |\vec s|=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5 \) m.
common_mistakes: Applying the same number to both the x- and y-components instead of treating them independently.
Forgetting the factor of \( \dfrac12 \) in the displacement formula, or forgetting the acceleration term entirely.
Confusing the direction of displacement with the direction of velocity — these are generally different at any given instant.

topics.name: Projectile Motion
topics.summary: Projectile motion is the two-dimensional motion of an object launched with speed \( u \) at angle \( \theta \) to the horizontal, moving under gravity alone (\( a_x=0 \), \( a_y=-g \)). Three formulas describe it, and mixing them up is the most common source of error: the time of flight is \( T=\dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g} \) (a single power of \( \sin\theta \)), the maximum height is \( H=\dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g} \) (a squared sine), and the horizontal range is \( R=\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g} \) (a doubled angle). The horizontal velocity component \( u\cos\theta \) never changes throughout the flight, since there is no horizontal acceleration — this is exactly why the speed at the highest point equals \( u\cos\theta \), not zero (only the vertical component vanishes there). When a projectile is launched from a height above the ground, or when the time to reach a particular height during the flight is needed, the general quadratic \( y=u\sin\theta\,t-\dfrac12gt^2 \) (with any extra launch height added) must be solved directly, rather than relying on the ground-to-ground shortcut formulas.
topics.worked_example: A ball is launched at \( u=20 \) m/s, \( \theta=30^\circ \), with \( g=10 \) m/s\( ^2 \): \( T=\dfrac{2\times20\times\sin30^\circ}{10}=2 \) s, \( H=\dfrac{20^2\times\sin^230^\circ}{2\times10}=5 \) m, \( R=\dfrac{20^2\times\sin60^\circ}{10}=20\sqrt3 \) m.
common_mistakes: Mixing up which power or multiple of \( \sin\theta \) belongs to which formula — a single \( \sin\theta \) for \( T \), a squared \( \sin^2\theta \) for \( H \), and a doubled \( \sin2\theta \) for \( R \).
Treating the horizontal velocity as if it changes during flight, or applying \( g \) to the horizontal component instead of only the vertical one.
Using the ground-level time-of-flight formula for a projectile launched from a height above the ground, where it no longer applies.

topics.name: Uniform Circular Motion
topics.summary: In uniform circular motion, a particle moves at constant SPEED around a circle of radius \( r \), but its VELOCITY is not constant, since its direction keeps changing at every instant. This means there is always a nonzero acceleration, called the centripetal acceleration, given by \( a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}=\omega^2r \), directed toward the centre of the circle — never outward, and never zero, no matter how steady the speed is. The angular speed \( \omega \) relates to the period \( T \) (the time for one full revolution) via \( \omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T} \), and to the linear speed via \( v=r\omega \). Since the motion is uniform, equal angles are swept in equal times, so the time to cover any fraction of a revolution is exactly that same fraction of the period. A common practical unit is revolutions per minute (rpm), which must first be converted to rad/s (\( \omega=2\pi\times\text{rpm}/60 \)) before it can be used in any of these formulas — forgetting either the \( 2\pi \) or the division by 60 is a frequent source of error.
topics.worked_example: A particle moves in a circle of radius \( 2 \) m with period \( 4 \) s: \( \omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2} \) rad/s, \( v=2\times\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\pi \) m/s, and \( a_c=\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)^2\times2=\dfrac{\pi^2}{2} \) m/s\( ^2 \).
common_mistakes: Assuming constant speed means zero acceleration, ignoring that the velocity's direction is constantly changing.
Confusing the true (centripetal, inward) direction of the acceleration with the outward-pointing centrifugal force felt in a rotating frame.
Using the wrong formula, such as \( v/r \) or \( v^2r \), instead of \( v^2/r \) for the centripetal acceleration.

topics.name: Relative Velocity in Two Dimensions
topics.summary: The velocity of object A relative to object B is \( \vec v_{AB}=\vec v_A-\vec v_B \) — always the first-named object's velocity minus the second's. Reversing this order gives the exact negative (opposite) vector, not the same answer, so the order can never be swapped carelessly. This single rule underlies every relative-velocity scenario in this topic: a boat crossing a river combines its velocity relative to the water with the water's velocity relative to the ground, using the chain rule \( \vec v_{boat,ground}=\vec v_{boat,water}+\vec v_{water,ground} \) (itself a rearrangement of the same subtraction rule); rain appears to fall at an angle to a walking person purely because of the person's own motion; and an aircraft's ground speed depends on how its airspeed vector combines with the wind. For river-crossing problems specifically, only the velocity component perpendicular to the bank determines the crossing time — the downstream drift carries the boat sideways but never slows its progress across. Every problem in this topic is ultimately a vector-addition or vector-subtraction exercise applied to real, moving reference frames.
topics.worked_example: Car A has velocity \( \vec v_A=5\,\hat i+3\,\hat j \) m/s and car B has velocity \( \vec v_B=2\,\hat i+1\,\hat j \) m/s. Then \( \vec v_{AB}=\vec v_A-\vec v_B=3\,\hat i+2\,\hat j \) m/s.
common_mistakes: Reversing the subtraction order (computing \( \vec v_{BA} \) instead of \( \vec v_{AB} \)), which gives the exact opposite vector.
Adding the two velocities instead of subtracting them.
Using the full resultant (ground) speed, including any drift, instead of just the across-component when finding a river-crossing time.

questions.topic: Vectors: Representation, Addition, Subtraction, and Resolution into Components
questions.question: A displacement vector of magnitude \( 10 \) m makes an angle \( 30^\circ \) with the positive x-axis. What are its x- and y-components?
questions.explanation:
The x-component is \( A\cos\theta \) and the y-component is \( A\sin\theta \).

\( A_x=10\cos30^\circ=5 \sqrt3 \) m, \( A_y=10\sin30^\circ=5 \) m.

So the vector is \( 5 \sqrt3\,\hat i+5\,\hat j \) m.
questions.hint: Drop a perpendicular from the vector's tip to the x-axis to form a right triangle; \( \cos\theta \) gives the base, \( \sin\theta \) gives the height.
distractor_logic: Uses \( \sin\theta \) for the x-component and \( \cos\theta \) for the y-component instead of the other way round.
Forgets to multiply the horizontal side by \( \cos\theta \), leaving the x-component equal to the full magnitude.
Resolves the magnitude correctly but assigns the y-component a negative sign, as though the vector pointed below the axis.

questions.question: Two forces of magnitudes \( 5 \) N and \( 3 \) N act on a body along the same direction (the angle between them is \( 0^\circ \)). Find the magnitude of the resultant force.
questions.explanation: Since the two vectors are collinear and point the same way, their magnitudes simply add: \( R=A+B=5+3=8 \) N. The general law \( R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta} \) reduces to this only because \( \cos0^\circ=1 \).
questions.hint: Collinear vectors add directly along the line of action — check whether they point the same way or opposite ways before combining them.
distractor_logic: Applies the rule for the opposite case (adds when they are opposite, or subtracts when they are aligned).

Uses the general two-vector law \( \sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta} \) meant for non-collinear vectors, which is unnecessary and wrong here since \( \cos0^\circ \) or \( \cos180^\circ \) already collapses it to a simple sum or difference.
Averages the two magnitudes instead of combining them.

questions.topic: Motion in a Plane with Constant Velocity and Constant Acceleration
questions.question: A particle moves with a constant velocity \( \vec v=3\,\hat i+4\,\hat j \) m/s for a time of \( 2 \) s. Find its displacement.
questions.explanation:
For constant velocity, \( \vec s=\vec v\,t \), applied component-wise.

\( s_x=3\times2=6 \) m, \( s_y=4\times2=8 \) m, so \( \vec s=6\,\hat i+8\,\hat j \) m.
questions.hint: Multiply each component of the velocity vector by the time separately — the x- and y-motions don't mix.
distractor_logic: Swaps the x- and y-components of the displacement.
Multiplies only the x-component by the time and leaves the y-component as the bare velocity value.
Gets the x-component right but flips the sign of the y-component.

A unit vector has magnitude 1, so \( a^2+\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^2=1 \).

\( a^2=1-\dfrac{9}{25}=\dfrac{16}{25} \), so \( a=\dfrac{4}{5} \).

questions.question: Two vectors \( \vec A \) and \( \vec B \), each of magnitude \( 5 \) N, are inclined at \( 60^\circ \) to each other. Through what angle \( \beta \) from \( \vec A \) does the resultant point?
questions.explanation:
When two vectors have equal magnitude, their resultant always bisects the angle between them (this follows directly from \( \tan\beta=\dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta} \) with \( A=B \), which simplifies to \( \tan\beta=\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2} \)).

So \( \beta=\dfrac{60^\circ}{2}=30^\circ \).
questions.hint: Equal magnitudes make the parallelogram of vectors a rhombus, and a rhombus's diagonal bisects its angle.
distractor_logic: Assumes the resultant points along the same direction as the full angle between the vectors, not its bisector.
Divides the angle by 3 instead of 2, misremembering the bisector fraction.
Doubles the angle instead of halving it.

questions.question: A particle starts with velocity \( \vec u=2\,\hat i+0\,\hat j \) m/s. For the first \( 2 \) s it has a constant acceleration \( \vec a_1=1\,\hat i+2\,\hat j \) m/s\( ^2 \); for the next \( 3 \) s it has a constant acceleration \( \vec a_2=0\,\hat i-1\,\hat j \) m/s\( ^2 \). Apply \( \vec v=\vec u+\vec a\,t \) twice in sequence, feeding the end of stage 1 in as the start of stage 2.

Stage 2: \( \vec v_2=\left(4\,\hat i+4\,\hat j\right)+\left(0\,\hat i-1\,\hat j\right)\times3=4\,\hat i+1\,\hat j \) m/s.
questions.hint: Work through the two stages one at a time — the velocity at the end of stage 1 becomes the starting velocity for stage 2.
distractor_logic: Applies only the second acceleration, over the full combined time, ignoring what happened during stage 1.
Stops after stage 1 and forgets to apply the second acceleration at all.
Adds both accelerations together and applies the sum only over the first time interval.

questions.question: A ball is thrown from the top of a tower of height \( 15 \) m, with speed \( 20 \) m/s at an angle of \( 30^\circ \) above the horizontal. Taking \( g=10 \) m/s\( ^2 \) and the ground as \( y=0 \), find the time it takes to hit the ground.

Taking up as positive and the launch point at height \( h \), the height at time \( t \) is \( y=h+u\sin\theta\,t-\dfrac12gt^2 \). Setting \( y=0 \) and solving the quadratic for the positive root:

questions.question: A projectile launched at \( 30^\circ \) to the horizontal has the same range as one launched at \( 60^\circ \) with the same speed (complementary angles). Find the ratio \( T_1/T_2 \) of their times of flight.

questions.question: A boat that can travel at \( 10 \) km/h in still water must cross a river flowing at \( 5 \) km/h, heading upstream at just the right angle so that it lands directly opposite its starting point (no net drift). Find its resultant speed across the river.

\( \sin\theta=\dfrac{5}{10}=\dfrac{1}{2} \), so \( \theta=30^\circ \), giving \( v_{across}=10\cos30^\circ=5 \sqrt3 \) km/h.

questions.question: Rain falls vertically downward at \( 10 \) m/s. A man walks horizontally at \( 10*sqrt(3) \) m/s. At what angle from the vertical should he tilt his umbrella to stay dry?

The rain's velocity relative to the man is \( \vec v_{rain}-\vec v_{man} \). Since the man's motion is horizontal and the rain's fall is vertical, these combine at right angles: the angle from the vertical is \( \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{v_{man}}{v_{rain}}\right) \).

\( \tan\theta=\dfrac{10*sqrt(3)}{10}=\sqrt3 \), so \( \theta=60^\circ \) from the vertical.

The ground velocity is the vector sum of the aircraft's velocity relative to the air and the wind's velocity relative to the ground: \( \vec v_{ground}=\vec v_{air}+\vec v_{wind} \), so \( v_{ground}=\sqrt{v_{air}^2+v_{wind}^2+2v_{air}v_{wind}\cos\theta} \).

\( v_{ground}=\sqrt{5^2+3^2+2\times5\times3\times\cos60^\circ}=7 \) km/h.

The ground velocity is the vector sum of the aircraft's velocity relative to the air and the wind's velocity relative to the ground: \( \vec v_{ground}=\vec v_{air}+\vec v_{wind} \), so \( v_{ground}=\sqrt{v_{air}^2+v_{wind}^2+2v_{air}v_{wind}\cos\theta} \).

\( v_{ground}=\sqrt{10^2+5^2+2\times10\times5\times\cos120^\circ}=5 \sqrt3 \) km/h.
questions.hint: This is a vector addition (the wind adds to the aircraft's own velocity) — use \( \sqrt{v_{air}^2+v_{wind}^2+2v_{air}v_{wind}\cos\theta} \), not a plain sum or difference.

Subtracts the two speeds as scalars, ignoring the angle between them.
Swaps cosine for sine inside the resultant formula.

questions.question: A ball is launched from the ground with velocity \( \vec u=5\,\hat i+10\,\hat j \) m/s (\( \hat i \) horizontal, \( \hat j \) vertical), with \( g=10 \) m/s\( ^2 \). Find the maximum height it reaches.

The height formula \( H=\dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g} \) really just needs the vertical component of the launch velocity, since \( u\sin\theta=u_y \): \( H=\dfrac{u_y^2}{2g} \). The horizontal component \( u_x \) plays no role in the height at all.

questions.topic: Motion with Constant Acceleration and Projectile Motion
questions.question: A ball is projected from the ground with speed \( 10 \) m/s at \( 30^\circ \) to the horizontal (\( g=10 \) m/s\( ^2 \)). Treating this as general plane motion with constant acceleration \( \vec a=(0,-10) \) m/s\( ^2 \), find the speed of the ball at \( t=0.5 \) s.
questions.explanation:
Projectile motion is just constant-acceleration motion in a plane with \( a_x=0 \) and \( a_y=-g \). So \( \vec v=\vec u+\vec a\,t \) gives \( v_x=u\cos\theta \) (unchanged) and \( v_y=u\sin\theta-gt \), then \( |\vec v|=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2} \).

\( v_x=10\cos30^\circ=5 \sqrt3 \) m/s, \( v_y=10\sin30^\circ-10\times0.5=0 \) m/s, \( |\vec v|=5 \sqrt3 \) m/s.
questions.hint: Apply the general 2D formula \( \vec v=\vec u+\vec a\,t \) with \( \vec a=(0,-g) \) — gravity only ever acts on the vertical component.
distractor_logic: Reports the launch speed unchanged, as though the constant acceleration had no effect at all.
Adds \( gt \) to the vertical component instead of subtracting it.
Applies gravity's effect to the horizontal component instead of the vertical one — but \( a_x=0 \) always in projectile motion.

questions.question: A particle moves in uniform circular motion of radius \( 5 \) m, with centripetal acceleration of magnitude \( 20 \) m/s\( ^2 \). The centripetal acceleration always points from the particle toward the centre — the exact opposite direction to the particle's position vector \( (\cos\theta,\sin\theta) \) from the centre. So \( \vec a_c=-a_c(\cos\theta\,\hat i+\sin\theta\,\hat j) \).

questions.hint: The word 'centripetal' means centre-seeking — the acceleration vector always points opposite to the particle's position vector from the centre, never along it.

Corrects the x-component's direction but leaves the y-component pointing outward, mixing the two conventions.

questions.topic: Uniform Circular Motion and Relative Velocity
questions.question: Two particles A and B move in uniform circular motion on the same circle of radius \( 5 \) m, at the same constant speed \( 10 \) m/s, always remaining diametrically opposite each other. At an instant when A moves due north and B (on the opposite side) therefore moves due south, find the velocity of A relative to B.

Taking north as \( +\hat j \): \( \vec v_A=(0,10) \) m/s and \( \vec v_B=(0,-10) \) m/s (B moves due south). \( \vec v_{AB}=\vec v_A-\vec v_B=(0,10)-(0,-10)=(0,210) \) m/s — the two velocities don't cancel, they add, because B moves opposite to A.

\( v_{AB}=2\times10=20 \) m/s (due north).
questions.hint: Even though A and B have the same speed, they move in opposite directions at this instant — write out \( \vec v_A-\vec v_B \) in components rather than assuming equal speeds cancel.
distractor_logic: Wrongly assumes that because the speeds are equal, the relative velocity must be zero.
Reports just the common speed \( v \), missing that B's velocity is in the opposite direction and doesn't simply cancel out of the subtraction.
Gets the right magnitude but computes \( \vec v_{BA} \) (B relative to A) instead of \( \vec v_{AB} \), the reversed vector.

questions.question: Particle P moves in a straight line with constant acceleration \( \vec a=6\,\hat i+8\,\hat j \) m/s\( ^2 \). Particle Q moves in uniform circular motion of radius \( 5 \) m at constant speed \( 10 \) m/s. Find the ratio of P's acceleration magnitude to Q's.
questions.explanation:
P's acceleration magnitude is \( |\vec a|=\sqrt{a_x^2+a_y^2} \). Q's acceleration, even though its speed never changes, is the centripetal acceleration \( a_c=v^2/r \) (never zero, since its direction keeps changing).

\( |\vec a|=\sqrt{6^2+8^2}=10 \) m/s\( ^2 \), \( a_c=\dfrac{10^2}{5}=20 \) m/s\( ^2 \), so the ratio is \( \dfrac{1}{2} \).
questions.hint: Q's speed being constant does NOT mean its acceleration is zero — uniform circular motion still has centripetal acceleration \( v^2/r \) directed toward the centre.
distractor_logic: Inverts the ratio, giving Q's acceleration over P's instead of P's over Q's.
Uses \( v/r \) instead of \( v^2/r \) for the circular motion's acceleration.
Adds P's acceleration components as plain numbers instead of combining them with the Pythagorean rule.

Ignores the acceleration entirely, using only \( s=ut \) for each component.
Swaps the resolved x- and y-components of \( \vec u \) before combining them with the acceleration terms.

questions.question: A ball is projected from the ground with speed \( 20 \) m/s at \( 30^\circ \) to the horizontal (\( g=10 \) m/s\( ^2 \)). questions.question: A ball's velocity relative to the surrounding air is \( \vec v_A=4\,\hat i+10\,\hat j \) m/s. The wind itself blows with velocity \( \vec v_{wind}=2\,\hat i+3\,\hat j \) m/s. Adds \( \dfrac12gt^2 \) instead of subtracting it, as though gravity acted upward.

questions.question: Particles A and B move at the same constant speed \( 10 \) m/s around the same circle (uniform circular motion). At a certain instant, A is at angular position \( 0^\circ \) and B is at angular position \( 60^\circ \) (both measured from the centre, from the positive x-axis). Each particle's velocity is tangential — perpendicular to its radius — so it points along \( (\text{position angle}+90^\circ) \). Resolve both into components, then apply \( \vec v_{AB}=\vec v_A-\vec v_B \).

\( \vec v_A=0\,\hat i+10\,\hat j \) m/s (tangent at \( 90^\circ \)), \( \vec v_B=-5 \sqrt3\,\hat i+5\,\hat j \) m/s (tangent at \( 150^\circ \)).

\( \vec v_{AB}=\vec v_A-\vec v_B=5 \sqrt3\,\hat i+5\,\hat j \) m/s.

Adds the two velocity vectors instead of subtracting them.
Subtracts correctly but swaps the x- and y-components of the result.

questions.topic: Motion with Constant Acceleration and Projectile Motion
questions.question: At the highest point of a projectile's trajectory, which statement correctly describes its velocity and acceleration?
options: both the velocity and the acceleration are zero at the highest point
the velocity is purely horizontal, but the acceleration is still \( g \), directed downward
the velocity is zero, but the acceleration is still \( g \), directed downward
the acceleration briefly points upward as the ball starts to fall back down
questions.explanation: Projectile motion has constant acceleration \( \vec a=(0,-g) \) throughout the entire flight — this never changes, not even momentarily at the top. What DOES become zero at the highest point is only the vertical component of velocity; the horizontal component \( u\cos\theta \) is unaffected and never zero (for an oblique launch).
questions.hint: Constant acceleration means constant — it doesn't pause or reverse at the peak of the trajectory, even though the vertical velocity does momentarily vanish there.
distractor_logic: Confuses the momentary zero in vertical velocity with the ball's motion (and hence acceleration) stopping entirely.
Confuses the ball's momentarily-zero vertical velocity with its total velocity being zero, when the horizontal component is still present.
Assumes the direction of acceleration must switch to match the ball's change from rising to falling, when it is constant throughout.
